topic.name: Django REST Framework (seed slice)
topic.scope_description: A small hand-authored slice of DRF used to build and verify the app before the generator exists: serialization, views, routing, and the GET request lifecycle.

nodes.name: HTTP request/response cycle
nodes.description: A client sends an HTTP request (method, path, headers, body); the server returns a response (status code, headers, body). Everything DRF does sits on top of this exchange.

nodes.name: Django Model
nodes.description: A Python class mapping to a database table via the Django ORM. Each instance is a row; fields are columns.

nodes.name: QuerySet
nodes.description: A lazy, chainable representation of a database query over a model. It is not evaluated until iterated, sliced, or cached.

nodes.name: Serializer
nodes.description: Converts model instances or querysets to native Python types (then JSON) for output, and validates/converts incoming data for input.

nodes.name: Serializer validation
nodes.description: On input, a serializer runs field-level and object-level validation; is_valid() populates validated_data or errors before any save.

nodes.name: APIView
nodes.description: DRF's class-based view. Maps HTTP methods to handler methods (get, post, ...), wraps the request/response, and applies authentication, permissions, and throttling.

nodes.name: Response object
nodes.description: DRF's Response takes serialized (native Python) data and renders it into the negotiated content type, attaching the HTTP status code.

nodes.name: URL routing / dispatch
nodes.description: Django matches the request path against URL patterns and dispatches to the matched view callable.

nodes.name: Router (DRF)
nodes.description: Automatically generates URL patterns for a ViewSet, wiring standard actions (list, retrieve, create, ...) to routes.

nodes.name: GET request lifecycle through a DRF endpoint
nodes.description: The ordered path a GET takes: URL routing dispatches to a view, the view builds a queryset, a serializer converts it, and a Response renders the result back to the client.

questions.prompt: An HTTP request carries a method, path, headers, and body; the server returns a response with a status code, headers, and a ____.
questions.expected_answer: body

questions.prompt: Explain the HTTP request/response cycle and the main parts of each message.
questions.expected_answer: A client sends a request (method, path, headers, optional body). The server processes it and returns a response containing a status code, headers, and an optional body. It is stateless: each request is independent.

questions.prompt: A client calls GET /api/books/ and gets back JSON with status 200. Identify the request method, the path, and the response status code.
questions.expected_answer: Method GET, path /api/books/, response status code 200 (OK).

questions.prompt: A Django Model class maps to a database ____, where each instance is a row and each field is a column.
questions.expected_answer: table

questions.prompt: What is a Django Model and how does it relate to the database?
questions.expected_answer: A Model is a Python class mapping to a DB table via the ORM. Each instance corresponds to a row; declared fields correspond to columns. It provides a Python API for queries and persistence.

questions.prompt: You need to store books with a title and author. Sketch the Model fields you would declare.
questions.expected_answer: A Book(models.Model) with title = models.CharField(max_length=...) and author = models.CharField(...) (or a ForeignKey to an Author model).

questions.prompt: A QuerySet is ____: it is not evaluated until you iterate, slice, or cache it.
questions.expected_answer: lazy

questions.prompt: What is a QuerySet and what does its laziness mean in practice?
questions.expected_answer: A QuerySet is a chainable representation of a DB query over a model. Laziness means building/filtering it issues no SQL; the query runs only when the QuerySet is evaluated (iterated, sliced with a step, len/list, or cached).

questions.prompt: Book.objects.filter(author='Le Guin') has been assigned to a variable but never iterated. Has the database been queried yet? Why?
questions.expected_answer: No. filter() returns a lazy QuerySet; no SQL runs until it is evaluated (e.g., iterated or listed).

questions.prompt: On output a serializer converts model instances/querysets to native Python types; on input it validates and ____ incoming data.
questions.expected_answer: deserializes / converts

questions.prompt: Describe both directions a DRF serializer handles.
questions.expected_answer: Output: it serializes model instances or querysets into native Python datatypes that renderers turn into JSON. Input: it deserializes incoming data, runs validation, and exposes validated_data for saving.

questions.prompt: Given a Book queryset to return as JSON, what serializer argument lets one serializer handle many objects?
questions.expected_answer: Pass many=True (e.g., BookSerializer(queryset, many=True)) so it serializes a list of objects.

questions.prompt: Calling serializer.____() runs validation and populates either validated_data or errors.
questions.expected_answer: is_valid

questions.prompt: Explain how serializer validation works on input.
questions.expected_answer: On input you call is_valid(); the serializer runs field-level validators then object-level validate(). On success validated_data is populated; on failure errors is populated. You only save after is_valid() passes (often is_valid(raise_exception=True)).

questions.prompt: A POST sends an empty required title. What does is_valid() return and where does the message go?
questions.expected_answer: is_valid() returns False and the message goes into serializer.errors (e.g., {'title': ['This field is required.']}).

questions.prompt: In an APIView, an incoming GET is dispatched to the view's ____ method.
questions.expected_answer: get

questions.prompt: What does DRF's APIView provide over a plain Django view?
questions.expected_answer: It maps HTTP methods to handler methods (get/post/...), wraps incoming requests in DRF's Request and uses Response, and applies authentication, permissions, throttling, and content negotiation.

questions.prompt: You want a class-based endpoint that returns a list on GET and creates on POST. Which two methods do you implement on the APIView?
questions.expected_answer: get(self, request, ...) and post(self, request, ...).

questions.prompt: DRF's Response takes already-serialized native data and renders it into the negotiated ____ type.
questions.expected_answer: content

questions.prompt: What is the role of DRF's Response object?
questions.expected_answer: Response wraps serialized native Python data plus an HTTP status code, then defers rendering to the negotiated content type (usually JSON) via the configured renderer.

questions.prompt: Return serialized data with a 201 status after creating a resource. What do you pass to Response?
questions.expected_answer: Response(serializer.data, status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED).

questions.prompt: Django matches the request ____ against URL patterns to choose which view to call.
questions.expected_answer: path

questions.prompt: How does Django decide which view handles a request?
questions.expected_answer: It walks the URLconf patterns in order, matching the request path against each; the first match dispatches to that view callable, passing any captured parameters.

questions.prompt: A DRF Router auto-generates URL patterns for a ____, wiring standard actions to routes.
questions.expected_answer: ViewSet

questions.prompt: What problem does a DRF Router solve?
questions.expected_answer: It removes hand-written URL boilerplate by generating the standard URL patterns for a ViewSet's actions (list, retrieve, create, update, destroy) from a single register() call.

questions.prompt: How does a Serializer relate to a QuerySet in producing a JSON list response?
questions.expected_answer: The view builds a QuerySet (the data source); the Serializer (with many=True) consumes that QuerySet and converts each instance to native data for rendering. The QuerySet is used inside the serialization step.

questions.prompt: Explain the link between a QuerySet and a Serializer.
questions.expected_answer: A QuerySet supplies the model instances; a Serializer transforms them into output representations. The serializer depends on the queryset as its input but adds the conversion/validation layer.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of a GET through a DRF endpoint in order: Serializer, URL routing, Response, QuerySet, APIView.
questions.expected_answer: 1) URL routing/dispatch, 2) APIView handler, 3) QuerySet built, 4) Serializer converts, 5) Response renders.

questions.prompt: Walk through what happens to a GET request from URL to JSON in a DRF endpoint.
questions.expected_answer: URL routing matches the path and dispatches to the APIView's get(); the view builds a QuerySet for the data; a Serializer (many=True) converts those instances to native data; that data is wrapped in a Response which renders it to JSON with a 200 status.

questions.prompt: A list endpoint returns an empty [] with status 200 instead of the expected rows. Using the lifecycle, where would you look first?
questions.expected_answer: Trace the order: routing hit the right view? the QuerySet's filter is not excluding everything? the serializer used many=True? Most likely the QuerySet is empty (over-restrictive filter) since routing/serializer/response succeeded with a 200.
